name: Seguimiento comercial con IA - Diseña campañas para tus clientes.
description:
Muchas empresas acumulan contactos interesados, propuestas pendientes y clientes con los que han perdido el contacto. Dar seguimiento a esas relaciones requiere organización, contexto y mensajes que lleguen en el momento adecuado.

En este encuentro online veremos **cómo diseñar y ejecutar campañas de seguimiento de preventa y postventa con IA, y convertirlas en un servicio que puedas ofrecer a tus clientes.**
Trabajaremos con ejemplos de seguimiento de propuestas, recuperación de oportunidades, acompañamiento tras la compra y reactivación de clientes.

Recorreremos tanto el diseño de la campaña como los datos, la configuración del correo y los aspectos legales que debes revisar antes de activarla.

## Qué veremos

* Cómo identificar oportunidades de seguimiento en la base de leads y clientes de una empresa.
* Cómo diferenciar campañas de **preventa, postventa, reactivación y recompra.**
* Cómo segmentar contactos según su relación con el negocio, sus necesidades y sus interacciones anteriores.
* Cómo definir el objetivo, el mensaje, la frecuencia y las condiciones de salida de cada campaña.
* Qué aspectos revisar sobre **RGPD, LSSI, permisos de contacto y solicitudes de baja.**
* Cómo preparar dominios y buzones y qué papel tienen **SPF, DKIM y DMARC.**
* Cómo abordar el calentamiento de buzones y el volumen de envío según el caso, y cómo interpretar rebotes y quejas de spam.
* Cómo utilizar IA para preparar mensajes personalizados y secuencias con revisión humana.
* Cómo conectar las campañas con el CRM, gestionar respuestas y detener el seguimiento cuando corresponda.
* Cómo medir resultados: respuestas, oportunidades recuperadas, conversiones y recompra.
* Cómo convertir este proceso en un servicio con alcance, precio y responsabilidades definidos.
* Un framework práctico: **objetivo → segmento → datos y permisos → mensajes → ejecución → seguimiento → resultados.**

name: Oct 1 - APAC AI, ML and Computer Vision Meetup
description:
Join our APAC time-zone friendly virtual meetup to hear talks from experts on cutting-edge topics across AI, ML, and computer vision.

**Time, Date and Location**

6:00 PM - 8:00 PM PDT
Online. **[Register for the Zoom!](https://voxel51.com/events/apac-ai-ml-and-computer-vision-meetup-october-1-2026)**

**Beyond Exact Matches: Detecting Modified 3D Assets at Marketplace Scale**

How can a marketplace identify copied 3D assets when their orientation, geometry, or composition has changed? Drawing on my work in 3D content understanding at Roblox, this talk will explore multi-view and rotation-invariant representations for similarity and duplicate detection, including the challenges posed by deformed and fragmented copies.
It will examine how geometric and semantic signals can complement one another, and discuss practical trade-offs in evaluating detection quality and deploying these methods at scale. The presentation will draw on published patent applications and publicly shareable examples to offer practical lessons for engineers building visual search, content-understanding, and marketplace-safety systems.

*About the Speaker*

[Phani Harish Wajjala](https://www.linkedin.com/in/harish-wajjala-81a47119/) is a Principal Machine Learning Engineer at Roblox specializing in 3D computer vision, multimodal AI, and large-scale content understanding.

**Sign Language: Towards Sign Understanding for Robot Autonomy**

Navigational signs are common aids for human wayfinding and scene understanding, but are underutilized by robots. We argue that they benefit robot navigation and scene understanding, by directly encoding privileged information on actions, spatial regions, and relations.

Interpreting signs in open-world settings remains a challenge owing to the complexity of scenes and signs, but recent advances in vision-language models (VLMs) make this feasible. To advance progress in this area, we introduce the task of visual sign grounding, which parses locations and associated directions from signs, and maps them to region in the sign’s local environment.

Additionally, we present a baseline approach using VLMs, and demonstrate their promise on the task. We also outline different applications, such as localization and navigation, which benefit from the spatial-symbolic information encoded by navigational signs.

*About the Speaker*

[Nicky Zimmerman](https://www.linkedin.com/in/nicky-zimmerman-41b71694/) I am a postdoctoral researcher in NUS, working on open world navigation. My PhD thesis focused on human-inspired strategies for semantic localization and mapping. Previously, I worked as computer vision algorithm developer in General Motors and Intel.

**MeMo: Memory as a Model**

Large language models (LLMs) achieve strong performance across a wide range of tasks, but remain frozen after pretraining until subsequent updates. Many real-world applications require timely, domain-specific information, motivating the need for efficient mechanisms to incorporate new knowledge.

In this paper, we introduce MeMo (Memory as a Model), a modular framework that encodes new knowledge into a dedicated Memory model while keeping the LLM unchanged. Compared to existing methods, MeMo offers several advantages: (a) it captures complex cross-document relationships, (b) it is robust to retrieval noise, (c) it avoids catastrophic forgetting in the LLM, (d) it does not require access to the LLM’s weights or output logits that enabling plug-and-play integration with both open and proprietary LLMs, and (e) its retrieval cost is independent of corpus size at inference time.

Our experiments on three benchmarks, BrowseComp-Plus, NarrativeQA, and MuSiQue, show that MeMo achieves strong performance compared to existing methods across diverse settings.

*About the Speaker*

[Arun Verma](https://www.linkedin.com/in/arunverma100) is a Postdoctoral Associate at the Singapore-MIT Alliance for Research and Technology Centre, where he works with Daniela Rus, Armando Solar-Lezama, and Bryan Low.

description:

**Designing Multi‑Agent Systems: Sequential, Parallel, and Beyond with ADK**

Multi‑agent systems are powerful but choosing the wrong interaction pattern can quickly lead to fragile, slow, or expensive AI systems.
In this talk, we explore the core multi‑agent design patterns enabled by ADK, including sequential, parallel, and more advanced coordination models. Rather than focusing on tools alone, we’ll look at how to think architecturally about agent collaboration.

You’ll learn:

* When sequential agents are the right choice and when they become a bottleneck
* How parallel agents improve speed and coverage (and the trade‑offs they introduce)
* Common failure modes in poorly designed agent interactions
* Practical criteria for choosing the right pattern based on task, latency, and reliability

By the end of the session, you’ll have a clear mental model for designing multi‑agent systems that are intentional, scalable, and production‑ready.

*About the Speaker*

[Dr Roushanak Rahmat](https://www.linkedin.com/in/roushanakrahmat/) is an Enterprise AI Architect, Google Developer Expert (AI & Cloud), and recognized among the Top 100 Women in Tech (2025). With a PhD in Artificial Intelligence and over 15 years of experience, she specializes in designing and delivering enterprise-scale Generative AI, Agentic AI, and Deep Learning solutions that transform industries including healthcare, finance, energy, and public services.

**Privacy by Deployment: Architecting Agent-Driven Localization Workflows for Regulated Environments**

Most enterprise AI today is private by promise - a DPA, a SOC 2 report, or a contract clause that says, "we won't train on your data". For a regulated buyer, these are remedies after a breach, not controls that prevent or contain one. For organizations in healthcare, finance, defense, and government, privacy often requires stronger guarantees: data residency, customer-controlled execution, and, in some cases, operation within air-gapped environments.

This session demonstrates how agentic AI can automate a localization workflow while operating within these constraints. Using a real-world localization pipeline as an example, we will show how agentic systems can coordinate translation, review, quality assurance, and content preparation tasks while incorporating human checkpoints for approval and oversight.

We will also walk through the architectural patterns that enable these workflows to run inside customer-controlled and air-gapped environments without transferring sensitive content outside the customer boundary. The session includes a live product demonstration.

Key Takeaways

* Architectural patterns for deploying agentic AI in air-gapped and customer-controlled environments
* How agentic systems can automate localization workflows while preserving critical human review and approval processes
* Practical considerations for operating agentic workflows in regulated environments with auditability and governance requirements

*About the Speaker*

[Shruti Joshi](https://www.linkedin.com/in/28shruti) is building an AI powered secure localization stack for regulated industries such as healthcare, legal, finance that cannot send their content to a typical hosted SaaS. She brings 12+ years of engineering and architecture experience to the question this talk addresses: how do you make an agentic AI system deployable inside a regulated perimeter.

**MCP Is the Interface; Skills Are the Operating Discipline**

This talk shows how MCP and Agent Skills work together in practical agent systems. MCP gives agents a standard interface to tools, data, and workflows; skills encode the operating discipline that makes those connections reliable. Using a sanitized field-operations ledger as the case study, the talk walks through source intake, normalized state, uncertainty labels, role prompts, QA gates, and share-safe status drafting.

*About the Speaker*

[Chuck Hernandez](https://www.linkedin.com/in/chuck-hernandez/) is an AI engineering and client-delivery leader with 10+ years across software, data platforms, and enterprise implementation, including 3+ years shipping production GenAI systems.

**Agentic engineering is about good guidance.**

Garbage Inn. Is garbage out? This is true. For many input and output processes. In biological life and in computer systems, and equally true when working with LLM’s. The better the prompt, the better the context, the better the focus, And the better the contextual awareness, the better the quality of the output the LLM’s generates.
This is the governance, art and practice of what we like to call agentic engineering, something I've been practicing over the last year.

*About the Speaker*

[Dimitri Geelen](https://www.linkedin.com/in/dimitrigeelen/) builds things that don't need him once they're done. Frameworks, transitions, agentic systems — the measure of success is always the same: does it hold up when he leaves the room? He understands not just how to deploy, but what it takes for a new service to survive and scale inside a complex enterprise.

**Agent as Policy for Robotic Manipulation**

This talk will introduces how a general-purpose agent can directly drive a physical robot throughout task execution without any task-specific or environment-specific training. We introduce Agent as Policy (AGP), which places task planning and execution under the agent’s control.

*About the Speaker*

[Xiaobai Liu](https://www.linkedin.com/in/xiaobai-liu-33598336/) is a Professor of Computer Science at San Diego State University (SDSU), where he directs the Machine Vision and Perception Lab. Prior to joining SDSU in 2015, he conducted research and taught at UCLA.

**Grounding Multimodal Open-World Learning for Physical AI**

Physical AI systems such as robots, unmanned vehicles, and embodied agents must perceive and reason about a world that is dynamic, unstructured, and rarely matches their training distribution. Yet most multimodal models remain brittle when confronted with novel objects, unseen conditions, and a messy unstructured environment.

This talk develops how grounding perception across modalities and environments can make open-world learning more robust for physically situated systems. Drawing on our recent work, I will highlight the core challenges of multimodal open-world learning including out-of-distribution detection, distribution shift generalization, and cascaded semantic grounding and point toward multimodal systems that stay reliable when deployed in the unpredictable open world.

*About the Speakers*

[Salimeh Sekeh](https://www.linkedin.com/in/salimeh-sekeh-65473344/) is an Associate Professor of Computer Science at San Diego State University (SDSU), where she directs the Sekeh Laboratory. Her recognition includes an NSF CAREER Award and a Cisco research gift (both 2022), and the Maine College of Engineering and Computing Early Career Research Award (2023), along with multiple industry and federal research awards.

[Mary Wisell ](https://www.linkedin.com/in/mary-isabelle-wisell/)is a second-year PhD student in the Sekeh Lab and leads the lab's work on environment-aware OOD detection and cascaded failure analysis for multimodal intelligence with several publications in top-tier Machine Learning and computer vision conferences.

name: AI × Decentralized Trust: Kickoff of the LFDT AI Working Group
description:
AI is already in our pull requests — and agentic AI needs exactly what we build. Let's talk about both.

AI has already arrived in our repositories. It writes patches, reviews pull requests, and is often the first thing a newcomer asks about a codebase they don't understand yet. At the same time, agentic AI is arriving from the other direction — as a use case. Autonomous agents need identities they can prove, credentials others can verify, and a way to pay each other for the things they consume. That is our home turf.

LFDT has no shared position on either side of this yet. This meeting launches the LFDT AI Working Group and sets its scope together with the people who will do the work.

We will open three questions:

**How do we use AI when building LFDT projects? What** is allowed, what has to be disclosed, and what does it mean for provenance, licensing, DCO sign-off, and security review? The Linux Foundation's existing generative AI guidance is the floor — the question is what our projects need on top of it.

**Can AI help us grow our communities?** Review bots like CodeRabbit, automated triage of good first issues, and onboarding assistants promise a shorter path from first-time contributor to committer. Do they actually deliver that, or do they just add noise for maintainers to clean up? And if we want them, who runs them and who pays?

**Where does our work connect to the AI world?** Two neighbours at the Linux Foundation matter most: the Agentic AI Foundation (MCP, goose, AGENTS.md) and the x402 Foundation, which stewards payments over HTTP for agents. Agentic identity and agent-to-agent commerce are exactly where DLT belongs — and where LFDT projects should be visible.

This is a kickoff, not a keynote. Bring your opinions, your objections, and the problems you already have. We want to leave with an initial scope, a meeting cadence, and named volunteers for the first work streams.

name: Policy-Checked, Attributable, Revocable, Provable AI Agent Authorization
description:
AI agents are entering production with long-lived API keys in their environment, broader access than any task needs, and no answer to the questions: Which agent performed this action? Under whose authority?

A single prompt injection, leaked credential, or runaway agent can quickly become a security incident. Security reviews delay deployments, and auditors are often left without sufficient evidence to understand what happened.

Existing security infrastructure was not designed for autonomous AI agents. Identity providers register agents but do not authorize every action, secret managers distribute credentials to workloads, and API gateways route requests without making authorization decisions.

This talk introduces Caracal, an open source AI authorization system currently being developed through the LFDT LFX Mentorship program and supported by GitHub, Microsoft, and Vercel. We'll discuss what authority means for AI agents, why authorization must move beyond credentials, and how we designed Caracal's architecture to provide policy-based authorization, attribution, revocation, and auditability for agent actions.

The session will cover:

* Why traditional API key and identity models are insufficient for AI agents
* What authority means in autonomous AI systems
* The architectural design behind Caracal
* Practical approaches to securing AI agents in production

The meetup will be presented by the Caracal team, Ryan Madhuwala and Shubham Sharma.

Our LFX mentees, Mohammad Ali Haider and Ashutosh Singh, will also present their work on the project. If you're interested in AI security and secure agent infrastructure, we'd be happy to have you join us.

The 2026 hiring backdrop is cooler than payroll headlines suggest. Fewer job openings, longer feedback cycles, more competition per role. Hiring managers have a problem: they need to reduce risk (hiring the wrong person) and build excitement (finding someone who'll succeed). Most interview advice teaches you to sound perfect, but perfect candidates sound identical. In a tighter market, that's a losing strategy.
**The Framework**
Job searching is risk mitigation + excitement building. This means:

* Understanding *why* they're hiring and what actual risk they're trying to solve
* Knowing your question types (STAR, hypothetical, personality) and what each one is actually asking
* Positioning yourself as the answer to *their* specific problem, not just answering the question perfectly
* Standing out in a sea of candidates who sound interchangeable

* How to decode what a hiring manager is really asking beneath the surface question
* How to structure answers that reduce their risk and build their confidence

* How to tell stories that prove you can solve their specific problem

* Job seekers getting interviews but not offers

Framework + execution. You'll learn the structure, see examples of what works and what doesn't, and walk through how to adapt your approach to different question types and hiring contexts.

name: From Counter.Inc() to a billion series
description:
Add a counter. Two lines and you can finally see how often your service fails.

Then you add a label to tell failure reasons apart and the counter becomes genuinely useful. You can now see why it's failing.
So you start adding more labels, one for the kind of user, one for the value of the operation. Each one seems reasonable and enables rich queries and alerts.

This talk follows that counter all the way down: from instrumenting a Go service, to how Prometheus scrapes and stores your data, to building a horizontally scalable distributed metrics database as you go from just one counter to billions of them.

You don't need to know anything about observability to attend this session!
